content: The population under study faces significant challenges related to mental health, as documented in prior research. The integration of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services with HIV care has been shown to reduce transmission rates effectively. This integration is critical not only from a health and reproductive standpoint but also from a rights-based perspective. However, despite increased emphasis on integrating SRH and HIV services for adolescents, there is limited evidence to confirm whether this integration is being implemented in practice and, if so, to what extent. Shroufi et al. (2013) have argued that adolescent-friendly programming can improve both enrollment rates and treatment retention. However, the extent to which adolescent-friendly services are being provided beyond specialized centers remains unclear. Linkages with community-based initiatives have been shown to enhance the reach of target populations, optimize resource utilization, improve local capacity and commitment to health interventions, and strengthen community responsiveness to emerging health issues. The growing number of HIV-infected children surviving into adolescence necessitates a targeted approach that considers their unique developmental stage and the challenges associated with transitioning into adulthood. Many of these challenges remain poorly understood, and the degree to which they are being addressed is uncertain. This study aims to explore the availability of specialized and appropriate HIV treatment and care services for adolescents in health facilities across 23 countries in sub-Saharan Africa. The study employed a cross-sectional survey design, incorporating both quantitative and qualitative elements. A total of 218 health facilities from 23 countries across four sub-Saharan regions were surveyed. These countries included Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Guinea, Nigeria, the Republic of Congo, and Senegal (West/Central Africa); Burundi, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, and Uganda (East Africa); and Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Zambia, and Zimbabwe (Southern Africa). The largest number of facilities surveyed were from Nigeria (44 facilities), Kenya (35 facilities), and South Africa (18 facilities). The sample was primarily drawn from the PATA network health facilities, with additional responses sought from other networks such as the South Saharan Social Development Organization, the Elizabeth Glaser Pediatric AIDS Foundation, and the Clinton Health Access Initiative. These additional networks were approached to increase the sample size, and introductory emails with survey links were forwarded to clinics within these organizations. Of the 218 facilities surveyed, 130 (60%) were from the PATA network, while the remaining 88 (40%) were sourced through other networks. In terms of health facility location, 50% of the sample was based in urban settings, 17% in peri-urban areas, and 33% in rural areas. Most surveys were completed by doctors/clinicians (34%), followed by nurses (21%) and administrators/managers (19%). The mean number of adolescents in care at each clinic was 367, with an average of 289 (79%) of these adolescents on antiretroviral therapy (ART). The estimated total number of HIV-infected adolescent patients in care across the sampled facilities was 80,072. The data collection surveys were developed through a review of the literature and consultations with experts and stakeholders. Two versions of the survey were created: a shorter High-Level (HL) version with 31 items and a longer Deep Dive (DD) version with 61 items. Both versions were translated into French and Portuguese to facilitate participation from Francophone and Lusophone countries. Data collection was conducted via email, fax, telephone interviews, or a web-based survey platform. Most participants chose to complete the survey online due to the nature of some items requiring information from health facility records. The study identified several barriers to providing HIV treatment and care for adolescents. These included non-adherence to treatment, disclosure challenges, socio-economic factors (such as transportation costs and nutrition), stigma, myths and reliance on traditional medicine, poor caregiver support, loss to follow-up, and issues related to sexual and reproductive health. Other challenges included staff shortages, lack of adolescent-friendly services, medication side effects, and conflicts with school schedules. The study's limitations include the inability to gather detailed information on all thematic areas due to survey length constraints, incomplete responses from some participants, and the lack of inter-rater reliability calculations during data coding. Additionally, the results are not representative of all countries included in the research, as the analysis was limited to facilities within specific networks. The reliance on self-reported data from healthcare staff and the use of automated translation for non-English responses may have also affected the accuracy of the findings. Ethical considerations were addressed by informing participants of their right to withdraw from the study at any time without penalty. Consent was obtained before survey completion, and results were presented as aggregated data to preserve anonymity.
